8  Composition

Plotje’s poses let you combine whole plots into a single rendered image. A composite pose holds other poses and a layout; each sub-pose renders independently and the composite tiles them together.

This chapter walks through composition patterns from simple side-by-side arrangements to shared-scale marginal plots, using pj/arrange, pj/marginal and explicit composite-pose maps – compactly for simple cases, with a bit of literal map construction for nested layouts.

(ns plotje-book.composition
  (:require
   ;; Tablecloth -- dataset manipulation
   [tablecloth.api :as tc]
   ;; Kindly -- notebook rendering protocol
   [scicloj.kindly.v4.kind :as kind]
   ;; Plotje -- composable plotting
   [scicloj.plotje.api :as pj]
   ;; Rdatasets -- standard datasets
   [scicloj.metamorph.ml.rdatasets :as rdatasets]))

Side-by-Side via pj/arrange

The simplest composite: two independent poses, placed next to each other. pj/arrange takes a vector of poses and returns a composite. Each sub-pose has its own data, mapping, layers, and options. Coming from R, this is the same shape as patchwork’s p1 | p2 operator or cowplot’s plot_grid(p1, p2).

(pj/arrange
 [(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris) (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width {:color :species}))
  (-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris) (pj/lay-point :petal-length :petal-width {:color :species}))])

Pass {:cols 1} for a stacked arrangement (one column means each pose goes on its own row):

(pj/arrange
 [(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris) (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width {:color :species}))
  (-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris) (pj/lay-point :petal-length :petal-width {:color :species}))]
 {:cols 1})

A vector of vectors gives one row per inner vector. nil in place of a pose is a cell left empty: it keeps its place in the layout and draws nothing, so the other cells stay where they are.

(pj/arrange
 [[(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris) (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width {:color :species}))
   nil]
  [(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris) (pj/lay-point :petal-length :sepal-width {:color :species}))
   (-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris) (pj/lay-point :petal-length :petal-width {:color :species}))]])

pj/arrange also takes data first. A cell is then what one argument after the data is to pj/pose: a mapping such as {:x :sepal-length :y :sepal-width} is a panel drawing those two columns, and a single column, :sepal-length, is a panel drawing that column. A vector in the list of cells is never a cell: it is a row of cells, or an arrangement of its own. The layers are added afterwards, once, and are drawn in every cell:

(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/arrange [{:x :sepal-length :y :sepal-width}
                 {:x :sepal-length :y :petal-length}])
    pj/lay-point)

The two cells read one dataset, so the two cells share the :x axis on which both draw :sepal-length, and that axis is titled once (see Shared Scales below).

An arrangement can be built in steps, as a plot is built layer by layer. pj/arrange given an arrangement adds the new cells after its own and lays out the longer list as one call with that list would, so a third panel joins the row:

(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/arrange [{:x :sepal-length :y :sepal-width}
                 {:x :sepal-length :y :petal-length}])
    (pj/arrange [{:x :sepal-length :y :petal-width}])
    pj/lay-point)

A cell can also hold a row filter, {:where {:species "setosa"}}, and draw the rows that match it, as Cells that filter the data shows.

pj/arrange divides space equally among its sub-poses. For unequal splits (e.g., give the first cell twice the width of the second), construct the composite as an explicit map; the next section shows how.

Explicit Composite Poses

Under pj/arrange there is a plain-map composite pose. You can construct one directly when you need finer control – unequal weights, shared scales, or (in future work) non-plot leaves like text panels and key performance indicators.

An explicit :layout accepts :direction (:horizontal or :vertical) and :weights (one weight per sub-pose). Here the first cell gets twice the width of the second:

(def weighted
  (pj/pose
   {:layout {:direction :horizontal :weights [2 1]}
    :poses [{:mapping {:x :sepal-length :y :sepal-width}
             :layers [{:layer-type :point}]}
            {:mapping {:x :petal-length :y :petal-width}
             :layers [{:layer-type :point}]}]
    :data (rdatasets/datasets-iris)}))

pj/pose accepts a literal composite map and tags it for notebook auto-render – the same pose value the threaded API produces:

weighted

And printed, showing the composite’s structure – :layout with direction and weights at the top, then each sub-pose with its own :mapping and :layers, and the outer :data dataset:

(kind/pprint weighted)
{:layout {:direction :horizontal, :weights [2 1]},
 :poses
 [{:mapping {:x :sepal-length, :y :sepal-width},
   :layers [{:layer-type :point}]}
  {:mapping {:x :petal-length, :y :petal-width},
   :layers [{:layer-type :point}]}],
 :data
 https://vincentarelbundock.github.io/Rdatasets/csv/datasets/iris.csv [150 6]:

| :rownames | :sepal-length | :sepal-width | :petal-length | :petal-width |  :species |
|----------:|--------------:|-------------:|--------------:|-------------:|-----------|
|         1 |           5.1 |          3.5 |           1.4 |          0.2 |    setosa |
|         2 |           4.9 |          3.0 |           1.4 |          0.2 |    setosa |
|         3 |           4.7 |          3.2 |           1.3 |          0.2 |    setosa |
|         4 |           4.6 |          3.1 |           1.5 |          0.2 |    setosa |
|         5 |           5.0 |          3.6 |           1.4 |          0.2 |    setosa |
|         6 |           5.4 |          3.9 |           1.7 |          0.4 |    setosa |
|         7 |           4.6 |          3.4 |           1.4 |          0.3 |    setosa |
|         8 |           5.0 |          3.4 |           1.5 |          0.2 |    setosa |
|         9 |           4.4 |          2.9 |           1.4 |          0.2 |    setosa |
|        10 |           4.9 |          3.1 |           1.5 |          0.1 |    setosa |
|       ... |           ... |          ... |           ... |          ... |       ... |
|       140 |           6.9 |          3.1 |           5.4 |          2.1 | virginica |

The outer :data is inherited by both sub-poses. Each sub-pose has its own :mapping and :layers, and need not repeat the dataset. Subsequent examples in this chapter follow the same shape and show only the rendered plot.

Panels of Unequal Size

A histogram beside a scatter plot reads well narrower than the scatter, and a plot printed beside others may need panels of an exact size. An arrangement’s columns and rows of cells are equal by default; two pairs of plot options change that.

:col-weights and :row-weights give each column and row of panels its share of the plot, which keeps its :width and :height. The tick labels, strips and titles take their room first, and the weights share out the rest, so [2 1] draws the first panel twice as wide as the second:

(-> (rdatasets/ggplot2-mpg)
    (pj/arrange [{:x :displ :y :hwy} :hwy] {:col-weights [2 1]}))

:panel-width and :panel-height pin the panels in drawing units instead, and the plot’s size is worked out from them, as it is for a single plot. A number pins every column’s (row’s) panels, and a vector each column’s (row’s):

(-> (rdatasets/ggplot2-mpg)
    (pj/arrange [{:x :displ :y :hwy} :hwy] {:panel-width [300 150] :panel-height 200}))

Giving both kinds for one direction, :panel-width with :col-weights, reports an error. A facet over categories draws its panels at one size, so a vector there reports an error too; a facet over columns, such as a scatter plot matrix, takes them.

Shared Scales

Two cells that draw the same column are often read against each other – a marginal above a scatter, or one measurement shown for several groups – and then the two cells need one range on that axis. Whether cells share an axis by default depends on where they read their data. Cells that read the data of the pose holding them – a composite written with :data at its root, as above, or (pj/arrange data [...]) – share each axis on which they draw the same column, as the panels of a facet do. Cells that each carry data of their own, as in (pj/arrange [pose-a pose-b]), compute their own domains. :share-scales names the axes the cells share, whichever the default was, and the cells drawing the same column on such an axis are given one range. Below, each cell holds the rows of one species, and :x is shared:

(pj/arrange
 [(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
      (tc/select-rows #(= "setosa" (:species %)))
      (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width))
  (-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
      (tc/select-rows #(= "virginica" (:species %)))
      (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width))]
 {:share-scales #{:x}})

Both cells are drawn on one :x range, and each cell keeps its own :y range, because :share-scales names :x only. Only cells drawing the same column on :x share that axis: two cells drawing different columns there each keep their own range.

A date column pools the same way – an axis holds a date as a number of milliseconds, so the union across cells is defined, and the cells are ticked over it rather than each over its own dates. See Change Over Time.

What a Shared Axis Covers

A shared axis covers what the cells sharing it draw. What a cell draws is not always what its column holds: a stack of bars reaches the total of its segments, an error bar reaches its ends, and a smoothed line can dip below or rise above the points it was fitted to. Plotje measures each cell after its statistics have run, pools the measurements of the cells sharing the axis, and pads the pooled extent once. Every sharing cell then draws the same axis, and no mark is cut off at the edge of a panel.

Two shops below sell the same drinks in two halves of a year. No value in the :sold column reaches the tallest stack, and the shared :y axis of both cells reaches past that stack:

(def north-shop
  {:drink ["tea" "tea" "coffee" "coffee"]
   :half ["first" "second" "first" "second"]
   :sold [30 45 20 25]})
(def south-shop
  {:drink ["tea" "tea" "cocoa" "cocoa"]
   :half ["first" "second" "first" "second"]
   :sold [60 70 10 15]})
(pj/arrange
 [(-> north-shop (pj/lay-bar :drink :sold {:color :half :position :stack}))
  (-> south-shop (pj/lay-bar :drink :sold {:color :half :position :stack}))]
 {:share-scales #{:y}})

A rule or a band is covered too. A rule is drawn at a value written on its layer, which no column holds. Here one cell carries a limit beyond anything either species measures, and both cells reach it:

(def limit 8.5)
(pj/arrange
 [(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
      (tc/select-rows #(= "setosa" (:species %)))
      (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width)
      (pj/lay-rule-v {:x-intercept limit :color "firebrick"}))
  (-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
      (tc/select-rows #(= "virginica" (:species %)))
      (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width))]
 {:share-scales #{:x}})

A :domain that one cell specifies for a shared axis is the domain of every cell sharing that axis, since a shared axis is one axis. Below, the second cell specifies 0 to 10 for :x, and both cells are drawn on exactly that interval:

(pj/arrange
 [(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
      (tc/select-rows #(= "setosa" (:species %)))
      (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width))
  (-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
      (tc/select-rows #(= "virginica" (:species %)))
      (pj/lay-point {:x {:column :sepal-length :scale {:domain [0 10]}}
                     :y :sepal-width}))]
 {:share-scales #{:x}})

Two cells that specify different domains for one shared axis report an error naming both domains. To specify one domain for the cells, call pj/scale on the composite: (pj/scale composite :x {:domain [0 10]}) is the domain of every cell that specifies none of its own. On a shared axis, remove the :domain from the cells first: a cell that keeps its own domain reports the same error.

Columns That Share an Axis

A set of axes shares an axis among the cells that draw the same column on it. Two cells drawing different columns keep their own ranges, which is right when the columns are in different units and wrong when they measure one quantity. Highway mileage and city mileage are both in miles per gallon, and under #{:x :y} each panel still fits its own :y. Plotje prints a warning that no two cells share :y, naming the group form used next:

(-> (rdatasets/ggplot2-mpg)
    (pj/pose {:x :displ})
    pj/lay-point
    (pj/facet {:y [:hwy :cty]})
    (pj/options {:share-scales #{:x :y}}))

The full form of :share-scales is a map from an axis to the columns that go together on that axis. Cells whose columns go together share the axis:

  • :same-column – each column goes with itself only, which is what the set says;

  • a vector of groups of columns, such as [[:hwy :cty]] – the columns of a group go together, and a column in no group goes with itself only;

  • :all – every column goes together, so every cell shares the axis.

An axis the map leaves out is not shared. Here :x is shared as before, and the two mileage columns share :y, so a point at the same height is the same mileage in both panels:

(-> (rdatasets/ggplot2-mpg)
    (pj/pose {:x :displ})
    pj/lay-point
    (pj/facet {:y [:hwy :cty]})
    (pj/options {:share-scales {:x :same-column
                                :y [[:hwy :cty]]}}))

A group leaves the other columns alone. With engine displacement as a third panel, the mileage panels share a range and displacement keeps its own:

(-> (rdatasets/ggplot2-mpg)
    (pj/pose {:x :year})
    pj/lay-point
    (pj/facet {:y [:hwy :cty :displ]})
    (pj/options {:share-scales {:x :same-column
                                :y [[:hwy :cty]]}}))

The columns of a group may come from different datasets, which is how two poses that name one quantity differently are read against each other:

(pj/arrange
 [(-> {:day [1 2 3] :indoor [19.0 20.5 21.0]}
      (pj/lay-line :day :indoor))
  (-> {:day [1 2 3] :outdoor [4.0 9.5 14.0]}
      (pj/lay-line :day :outdoor))]
 {:share-scales {:y [[:indoor :outdoor]]}})

Columns that go together have to hold one type of value: numbers with numbers, dates with dates, categories with categories. A group holding a numeric column and a categorical one reports an error:

(try
  (-> (rdatasets/ggplot2-mpg)
      (pj/pose {:x :displ})
      pj/lay-point
      (pj/facet {:y [:hwy :drv]})
      (pj/options {:share-scales {:y :all}})
      pj/plan)
  (catch clojure.lang.ExceptionInfo e (ex-message e)))
":share-scales cannot share :y between these cells: columns :hwy, :drv have no one axis to be drawn on. The cells differ in column type: categorical and numerical. Cells sharing an axis must agree on the coordinate system, the column type (numerical, categorical or temporal) and the scale type (linear or log). Leave :y out of :share-scales, or name only the columns that go together."

A Shared Categorical Axis

A categorical axis is shared as the list of every category the sharing cells hold. A bar for tea then stands at the same place in each cell, and a cell with no rows for a category leaves the place of that category empty. The north shop sells no cocoa and the south shop no coffee; with :x shared, both cells list all three drinks. Each bar here is a drink’s total for the year:

(def north-totals
  {:drink ["tea" "coffee"] :sold [75 45]})
(def south-totals
  {:drink ["tea" "cocoa"] :sold [130 25]})
(pj/arrange
 [(-> north-totals (pj/lay-bar :drink :sold))
  (-> south-totals (pj/lay-bar :drink :sold))]
 {:share-scales #{:x :y}})

The two cells above have data of their own, so the categories come in the order of the cells: the drinks of the first cell, then the drink the second cell adds. Cells that are parts of one dataset – the panels of a facet, or the cells of a pose arranged over its own data – list the categories in the order of that dataset’s rows, which is the order the same plot draws them in when it is not split.

Count and Density Axes

A histogram draws a count on :y, and no column holds that count. An axis like this is shared by what is counted. Two histograms of one column share their count axis:

(pj/arrange
 [(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
      (tc/select-rows #(= "setosa" (:species %)))
      (pj/lay-histogram :sepal-length))
  (-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
      (pj/lay-histogram :sepal-length))]
 {:share-scales #{:y}})

Histograms of different columns keep a count axis each under a set of axes, as cells drawing different columns do. A group naming the columns shares their count axes:

(-> (rdatasets/ggplot2-mpg)
    pj/pose
    pj/lay-histogram
    (pj/facet {:x [:hwy :cty]})
    (pj/options {:share-scales {:y [[:hwy :cty]]}}))

A count, a density and the values of a column are measured in different units, so an axis holding one is never pooled with an axis holding another. {:y :all} shares every count axis with the other count axes, every density axis with the other density axes, and the axes of columns with each other. Below, the two histograms share one count axis and the scatter keeps the axis of its :hwy column:

(pj/arrange
 [(-> (rdatasets/ggplot2-mpg) (pj/lay-histogram :hwy))
  (-> (rdatasets/ggplot2-mpg) (pj/lay-histogram :cty))
  (-> (rdatasets/ggplot2-mpg) (pj/lay-point :displ :hwy))]
 {:share-scales {:y :all}})

A histogram normalized with {:normalize :density} draws a density, and shares with a density curve of the same column. A layer type added by an extension takes part by declaring what its statistic computes; see Extensibility.

Cells Drawn Flipped

:share-scales names an axis as it is drawn: :x is the horizontal axis and :y the vertical one. Under (pj/coord :flip) the column mapped to :y runs across the page, and #{:x} shares the axis that column is drawn on. (pj/scale and :x-label name the column’s own axis, whichever way that axis is drawn.) The totals of the two shops as flipped bars, sharing the horizontal axis:

(pj/arrange
 [(-> north-totals (pj/lay-bar :drink :sold) (pj/coord :flip))
  (-> south-totals (pj/lay-bar :drink :sold) (pj/coord :flip))]
 {:share-scales #{:x}})

Cells That Line Up

Each cell reserves the room its own y labels need, so a cell labelled in single digits comes out wider than a cell labelled in millions, and the axis the two share covers a different extent in each. :align-panels reserves the widest y-label pad and legend column any cell needs on all of them, so every cell gets the same drawing area:

(def readings
  {:t [1 2 3 4 5]
   :rate [1.0 2.0 3.0 2.0 4.0]
   :total [1200000.0 2400000.0 1800000.0 3100000.0 2600000.0]})
(pj/arrange
 [(-> readings (pj/lay-line :t :rate))
  (-> readings (pj/lay-line :t :total))]
 {:cols 1 :share-scales #{:x} :align-panels true})

Pair it with :share-scales where the cells are meant to be read against one another. pj/marginal sets both for you – the next section takes one apart.

A Facet Placed as a Cell

A facet shares both axes across its panels by default. Placed as a cell of an arrangement, the facet takes the arrangement’s options wherever it writes none of its own, as any cell does – and :share-scales is one of those options. Below, the arrangement shares :x across all its cells, and the facet over :drv, which writes no :share-scales, takes {:x :all} as its own: its three panels share :x and each keeps its own :y range.

(def drv-facet
  (-> (pj/pose nil :displ :hwy)
      (pj/facet :drv)))
(-> (rdatasets/ggplot2-mpg)
    (pj/arrange [[drv-facet]
                 [{:x :displ :y :cty} {:x :displ :y :hwy}]]
                {:share-scales {:x :all}})
    pj/lay-point)

Written on the facet, :share-scales replaces the arrangement’s value for the facet’s own panels, and they share :y again:

(-> (rdatasets/ggplot2-mpg)
    (pj/arrange [[(pj/options drv-facet {:share-scales #{:x :y}})]
                 [{:x :displ :y :cty} {:x :displ :y :hwy}]]
                {:share-scales {:x :all}})
    pj/lay-point)

Marginal Plots

The classic “scatter with top density” – a distribution strip beside the main plot – has a function of its own. pj/marginal takes a leaf pose and puts a distribution of one of its columns in a thin panel against one edge: the :x column above the panel, the :y column to its right.

(def marginal
  (-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
      (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width {:color :species})
      (pj/marginal :top)))
marginal

The strip shares the scatter’s x axis and keeps its own value scale. Its duplicate x ticks and axis title are dropped, since the axis below describes both panels, and the two drawing areas are aligned so a value sits at the same place in each – including here, where the scatter carries a legend and the strip does not.

The color mapping does not reach the strip. A marginal describes the pose’s :x column as a whole, so one grey curve is drawn over the three colored groups below it.

:histogram draws the distribution as bars instead of a curve, and :size sets the strip’s share of the height (0.25 by default):

(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width)
    (pj/marginal :top :histogram {:size 0.35}))

A marginal on the right

:right describes the pose’s :y column instead, in a strip beside the panel. The distribution is drawn under pj/coord :flip, so its value axis runs across the strip and its baseline stands at the left edge, against the scatter:

(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width {:color :species})
    (pj/marginal :right))

The strip shares the panel’s vertical axis. pj/marginal writes {:share-scales #{:y}} for a marginal on the right, and under the flip the strip’s :x column is the column drawn along that axis.

A :top marginal and a :right one line up on different edges. Two panels in a column share their left and right edges, so what has to agree is the room reserved for the y title and for the legend; two panels in a row share their top and bottom edges, so what has to agree is the room below them. :align-panels reserves whichever the layout calls for.

:bottom and :left are not drawn: a strip there would sit between the panel and the axis that describes it.

Marginals on both sides

pj/marginal adds one strip. For a marginal on each side, write the grid with pj/matrix: nil in a list of columns leaves a place with no column on that axis, so that cell draws the distribution of the other column, and the corner, nil on both axes, is left empty. The weights draw the marginals a third the size of the scatter:

(pj/matrix (rdatasets/ggplot2-mpg) [:displ nil] [nil :hwy]
           {:col-weights [3 1] :row-weights [1 3]})

What a marginal is made of

A :top marginal is a vertical composite with a shared x, which can also be written out. Four things make it up: the weights, the shared scale, the ticks and axis title suppressed on the strip, and :align-panels. Here are the first three:

(def marginal-by-hand
  (pj/pose
   {:share-scales #{:x}
    :layout {:direction :vertical :weights [1 3]}
    :poses [{:mapping {:x :sepal-length}
             :opts {:suppress-x-ticks true :suppress-x-label true}
             :layers [{:layer-type :density}]}
            {:mapping {:x :sepal-length :y :sepal-width :color :species}
             :layers [{:layer-type :point}]}]
    :data (rdatasets/datasets-iris)}))
marginal-by-hand

So the two drawing areas do not line up: the strip draws no legend, reserves no column for one, and comes out wider than the scatter below it. The density then sits at a different scale from the points it describes.

That is the fourth part, and the one pj/marginal adds: :align-panels in the composite’s own :opts. It plans every cell twice, the second time with the widest pad any of them needed as a floor, so each cell reserves what the others do – the y-label pad and the legend column for a column of cells, the room below for a row of them. pj/arrange takes :align-panels among its options, as above, and a written-out composite carries it in its own :opts. pj/options does not accept it – it is a composite’s own setting rather than a plot option:

(assoc-in marginal-by-hand [:opts :align-panels] true)

With the key in place the written-out form is the composite pj/marginal returns, up to the weights it computes from :size. Nothing in the shape is specific to distributions, so the same four parts serve any stack of panels read against one x axis.

A Small Dashboard

Composite poses can combine heterogeneous chart types. Here is a dashboard-style 2x2 layout: a histogram of sepal length, a boxplot of sepal width by species, a scatter of petal dimensions, and a density of petal length.

Each cell is built as its own leaf pose, then pj/arrange takes rows of cells and produces the 2x2 grid:

(def dashboard
  (pj/arrange
   [[(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris) (pj/lay-histogram :sepal-length))
     (-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris) (pj/lay-boxplot :species :sepal-width {:color :species}))]
    [(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris) (pj/lay-point :petal-length :petal-width {:color :species}))
     (-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris) (pj/lay-density :petal-length {:color :species}))]]))
dashboard

Four panels, each its own layer type. pj/arrange stacks the rows vertically; each row is laid out horizontally.

Drawing Layers with Different Data

A layer can carry its own :data, written in the layer’s mapping. This is how reference lines, predictions drawn over the data, and small datasets of labels attach to a plot. The layer reads every column from its own data: the columns it names, and the columns the pose’s mapping names.

A layer with data of its own is drawn on the pose’s panel, like any other layer of the pose. A separate panel for it comes from pj/arrange.

On the same panel

Here a base scatter gets a second set of points from another dataset, whose columns are named :x and :y:

(def overlay-base
  {:fitted   [1 2 3]
   :residual [1 2 3]})
(def overlay-other
  (tc/dataset {:x [0.5 1.5 2.5]
               :y [1.5 2.5 3.5]}))
(-> overlay-base
    (pj/lay-point :fitted :residual {:color "#377eb8"})
    (pj/lay-point :x :y {:color "#e6550d" :data overlay-other}))
Notestdout 
Note: pj/lay-point names :x on :x and :y on :y where this pose draws :fitted on :x and :residual on :y, and is drawn on the same panel; in 0.16.1 it was given a panel of its own. For a panel per pair of columns, write (pj/facet pose {:x [:fitted :x] :y [:residual :y]}), or arrange separate poses with pj/arrange.

One panel with six points – three from each layer. Layers paint in the order they were added – see Poses – so add the layer you want on top last.

Each axis is titled by both columns drawn on it, fitted, x and residual, y. Where the incoming columns are the same quantity under another name, renaming them to the pose’s columns with tc/rename-columns draws the same marks under one name per axis:

(-> overlay-base
    (pj/lay-point :fitted :residual {:color "#377eb8"})
    (pj/lay-point :fitted :residual
                  {:color "#e6550d"
                   :data (tc/rename-columns overlay-other
                                            {:x :fitted :y :residual})}))

A panel of its own

To draw the other dataset beside the base scatter, build each as a pose and arrange them:

(pj/arrange [(pj/lay-point overlay-base :fitted :residual {:color "#377eb8"})
             (pj/lay-point overlay-other :x :y {:color "#e6550d"})])

Each panel has three points and its own axis titles: the first shows fitted against residual, the second x against y.

Panels Clip Their Own Content

Each panel confines its marks to its own rectangle. A layer whose data runs past the panel’s domain – a reference line drawn well beyond the visible range, say – is clipped at the panel edge rather than painting across its neighbours. The clip is applied per panel, so a stacked arrangement reports one clip region per panel.

(def bounded
  (-> {:x [1 2 3 4 5] :y [10 20 15 25 18]}
      (pj/lay-point :x :y)
      (pj/lay-line {:data {:x [1 5] :y [-200 300]}})
      (pj/scale :y {:type :linear :domain [0 30]})))
(pj/arrange [bounded bounded] {:cols 1})

Notes on the Current Implementation

A few details about how composition renders today:

  • Cells with data of their own draw their own axes, titles and ticks, unless :share-scales asks them to share an axis. In (pj/arrange [pose-a pose-b] {:share-scales #{:x}}), and in cells that read the data of the pose holding them, as in (pj/arrange data [...]), a shared axis is titled once and its ticks are labelled on the outer cells only, as the panels of a facet do. Cells drawing different columns on one shared scale – under :all, or a group such as {:y [[:hwy :cty]]} – each keep their title and its tick labels. A cell drops its own with :suppress-x-ticks and :suppress-x-label in that cell’s :opts, which is what pj/marginal writes on the strip it builds. (A scatter plot matrix names its columns with strips in place of each panel’s axis titles, and labels its :x ticks along the bottom row only. A grid of cells written by hand gets these strips where it crosses a list of :x columns with a list of :y columns, as a matrix does: each grid column draws one :x column and each row one :y column. A grid whose grid columns each draw one :x column, while its rows do not each draw one :y column, titles that :x column once below each grid column, as a shared axis is titled.)

  • Plot-area edges may not line up across composite siblings, since each leaf reserves its own padding for axes and labels – two sub-poses with different label lengths, or one drawing a legend that its neighbour does not, produce visibly different panel widths. :align-panels on pj/arrange plans the cells against a common floor for both the y-label pad and the legend column, and pj/marginal turns it on (see Cells That Line Up).

  • Each cell has its own plot options. A cell is a pose, so pj/options, pj/scale and pj/coord written on it apply to that cell: one cell can be log-scaled and its neighbour linear, and each can have its own title. Written on the composite itself, a scale, a coordinate system or an option such as :x-label applies to every cell that does not set its own. The :title, :subtitle and :caption written there are drawn once, around the whole arrangement, and not in each cell. This is also the way around a limitation within one pose – two layers cannot read one aesthetic through different scales, but two cells can.

  • Cells that map the same column share one scale and one legend. If every leaf maps an aesthetic to the same column (e.g., :color :species in all cells), each cell is given one scale for it – the categories of all the cells together, or the range of all their values – and a single legend is drawn for the composite. A category is then the same colour, and a value the same shade, in every cell, even where the cells hold different data. A legend is drawn once, so its scale has to hold in every cell; cells with data of their own share an axis only where :share-scales names that axis. A cell that writes its own scale for the aesthetic keeps it, and each cell then draws its own legend. When the mappings disagree – or when only some leaves carry the aesthetic, as in the dashboard above – each leaf with that aesthetic draws its own legend.

  • Multi-row layouts go through pj/arrange. A row of rows is built by passing nested vectors of poses to pj/arrange (the dashboard example above shows the shape). A cell may be a composite itself, so an arranged pose can be arranged again and the cell draws its own grid. Cells of unequal size are written with :col-weights and :row-weights, or with :panel-width and :panel-height – see the section on panels of unequal size.

Below, both cells map :color to :species, and they hold different rows: the left cell holds setosa and versicolor, the right cell versicolor and virginica. Versicolor is drawn in the same colour in both, and the one legend lists all three species:

(pj/arrange
 [(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
      (tc/select-rows #(not= "virginica" (:species %)))
      (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width {:color :species}))
  (-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
      (tc/select-rows #(not= "setosa" (:species %)))
      (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width {:color :species}))])

A cell that is itself a composite draws its own grid. Here the left cell holds two panels of its own and the right cell holds one, so the arranged pose draws three panels in two columns:

(pj/arrange
 [(pj/arrange
   [(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
        (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width))
    (-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
        (pj/lay-point :petal-length :petal-width))]
   {:cols 1})
  (-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
      (pj/lay-histogram :sepal-length))])
